sections.h2: Who handles probate in North Carolina?
sections.html:
The elected clerk of superior court in each county serves as the probate judge. Clerks and their assistant clerks hear most estate matters, and a judge of the superior court only steps in when someone challenges a will in a caveat proceeding.

The register of deeds is a different office. It records deeds and collects the excise tax, but it does not open estates or issue letters. If you are selling a house that belonged to someone who died, you will deal with both offices, the clerk first and the register of deeds at the end.

sections.h2: Does a house have to go through probate in North Carolina?
sections.html:
Not always. The Judicial Branch explains that land and houses are generally not administered through the probate estate unless the will says otherwise or the house must be sold to pay the estate's debts.

State law still decides who holds title. Under G.S. 28A-15-2, title to a decedent's real property vests in the heirs at the moment of death, and property left by a valid probated will vests in the devisees, with that ownership relating back to the date of death. A personal representative can ask the clerk by petition to sell the real property to pay debts and other claims (G.S. 28A-17-1).

When there is no will, intestacy law decides who inherits. A spouse and children share in many cases, a spouse and parents share when there are no children, and a decedent with children but no spouse passes property to the children and the descendants of any child who has died. Because the rules differ by situation, ask the clerk of superior court in the decedent's county whether an estate should be opened before you sign a listing agreement.

sections.h2: What are the main probate routes for a North Carolina estate?
sections.html:
Source: NC Judicial Branch estates page and G.S. 28A-25-1
RouteWhen it fitsKey detail
Full administrationEstates that need a court-appointed representativeClerk issues letters; filing fee quoted at $120
Summary administrationSurviving spouse is the sole heir or deviseeAvailable with or without a will
Collection by affidavitSmall estates of personal propertyUp to $20,000, or up to $30,000 for a sole-heir spouse, after 30 days

The court system also offers an online guide-and-file service for year's allowance, summary administration and small estate administration. Your clerk's office can tell you which forms apply to your case.

sections.h2: How does a North Carolina small estate affidavit work?
sections.html:
An heir, a creditor or a public administrator can collect a decedent's personal property by affidavit at least 30 days after death, if the personal property less liens does not exceed $20,000 and no one has petitioned for or been granted letters. A surviving spouse who is the sole heir may use the process for an estate that, after reducing for the spousal allowance, runs above $20,000 but no higher than $30,000.

The affidavit goes to the clerk of superior court in the county where the decedent lived, and it must describe each tract of real property the decedent owned. The process itself covers personal property such as bank accounts and vehicles. If the estate holds a house, ask the clerk how that tract is to be handled and whether the sale needs a representative with letters.

sections.h2: How do you open a full estate with the North Carolina clerk?
sections.html:
Visit the clerk of superior court in the county where the person lived at death, since some clerks accept walk-ins and others require an appointment. Bring the original will if one exists, a certified death certificate, a completed application and preliminary inventory, and the $120 filing fee quoted by the court system.

  • An executor named in the will has top priority to receive letters, followed by any named substitute.
  • Without a will, the order runs from the surviving spouse to anyone receiving property under the will, then anyone who would inherit without one, next of kin, creditors, and finally a person of good character living in the county.
  • Out-of-state executors generally post a bond, and administrators post one unless an exception applies.
  • An estate can be reopened later if newly found property turns up.

A person who lived outside North Carolina can have an estate opened in any North Carolina county where property was left.

sections.h2: How long do creditors have to make claims in a North Carolina estate?
sections.html:
The notice period is at least three months from the first publication or posting. After letters issue, the personal representative must publish the notice once a week for four consecutive weeks in a newspaper qualified to carry legal advertisements, or post it where the statute allows if the county has none.

Known creditors get a copy by personal delivery or first class mail within 75 days after letters are granted, and the state's Division of Health Benefits is notified when the decedent received medical assistance. Ask the title company how it treats the claims period before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: What taxes and costs come up when selling an inherited North Carolina house?
sections.html:
North Carolina repealed its estate tax for people who die on or after January 1, 2013, so the state levies no estate tax on those estates. The recurring costs are property tax and the sale itself.

  • County property tax is due September 1 each year and picks up interest on January 6 when unpaid.
  • The seller pays the deed excise tax to the register of deeds before the deed is recorded, at $1.00 for each $500 of value or fractional part.
  • The register of deeds charges $26.00 to record a standard deed of up to 15 pages, and $4.00 for each page beyond that.

When a representative signs the deed, ask the title company which estate documents it needs to see, and request certified copies of the letters from the clerk in advance.

sections.h2: Which North Carolina office should you call first?
sections.html:
Start with the clerk of superior court in the decedent's home county, because that office knows whether a will has been filed and whether an estate is already open. Wills become public records once filed, and anyone may view one or request a copy for a fee. North Carolina law does not require a formal reading of a will, so families can move straight to filing it with the clerk and applying for letters.

If no will turns up, the court system suggests contacting clerks in other counties where the person once lived, since some people deposit a will for safekeeping with a clerk. Then call the register of deeds in the county where the house sits to learn how the deed is currently held and what recording will cost.

faqs.q: Who is the probate judge in North Carolina?
faqs.a: The elected clerk of superior court in each county acts as the probate judge. A superior court judge hears a caveat proceeding when a will's validity is challenged.

faqs.q: What is the North Carolina small estate affidavit limit?
faqs.a: It is $20,000 in personal property after liens for most estates. A surviving spouse who is the sole heir may use it up to $30,000, after any spousal allowance is subtracted.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to open an estate in North Carolina?
faqs.a: The court system quotes a $120 filing fee. Bring the will, a certified death certificate and the application and inventory forms.

faqs.q: Does North Carolina have an estate tax?
faqs.a: No. The state estate tax statutes were repealed effective January 1, 2013, and the repeal applies to people who die on or after that date.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house before the estate closes in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Possibly, but who can sign depends on the will and on the heirs. Title to real property vests in the heirs or devisees at death, and a representative can petition the clerk to sell for debts, so confirm the route with the clerk of superior court first.
